newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright tells Slovaks to "rejoin" democratic path.
newsitem.headline: Albright tells Slovaks to "rejoin" democratic path.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a speech in her native Prague on Monday, called on Slovakia to "rejoin the path" of democratic reform and earn a place in NATO alongside the Czech Republic.

Ending a tour of eastern Europe after last week's NATO summit, Albright made a special appeal to the eastern part of the former Czechoslovakia which has become a diplomatic outcast because of perceived shortcomings in democratic reforms.

Saying that the Clinton administration had promised to back all nations "between the Baltic and Black seas" which met NATO's criteria for membership, Albright added: "And it is our message today to the people of Slovakia."

"For it is our sincere hope that their nation will rejoin the path of true democratic reform and make itself a strong candidate for the second round of NATO enlargement," she told the leaders and diplomats gathered in Prague's Municipal House.
When Czechoslovakia peacefully split into separate states in 1993, Slovakia was still seen among the frontrunners for early NATO membership.

But the U.S. and other western allies have criticised Slovakia for four rocky years of opaque political infighting, problems in dealing with its large ethnic Hungarian minority, and major shortcomings in media and other reforms.

When NATO issued its first membership invitations to post-Communist states last week in Madrid, only Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic won the nod. Slovakia was not even mentioned among top prospects for future rounds. NATO has not yet specified when a second round of enlargement would take place but the first round is expected to be completed in 1999.
NATO agreed however that it would leave the door for eventual membership open to any applicant which fulfils its criteria of democracy, human rights, and a market economy.
Neither was Slovakia named among six countries to start talks on future membership in the European Union last week.

"I think the issue for all of us, NATO members and aspiring NATO members, is to make sure that Slovakia doesn't isolate itself," Albright, whose father was a Czechoslovak diplomat, told a joint news conference with Czech President Vaclav Havel.
"And that it is important that Slovakia understand what it takes to become a NATO member, which is democratisation, a market system and the capability to be an active participant."
Privately, U.S. officials blame Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's autocratic style of rule for the country's poor reputation in diplomatic circles.
Meciar, after the Madrid summit, complained that the NATO decision was unfair and used a different measure for his country than for other applicants.
Albright said she discussed what Slovakia would have to do to gain NATO membership with Meciar in Madrid.

Slovak President Michal Kovac told Reuters in an interview on Friday that he hoped "member countries of the European Union and NATO will not turn their backs on Slovakia" and instead intensively support "democratic forces" in the country.
